full_judgment:
18. The learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that when the defendants challenged identity. of the plaintiff and the genuineness of the Power of Attorney obtained from Jatindra Mahon Roy it was for the plaintiff to establish that the plaintiff Jatindra Mahon 'Roy is not a fictitious person rather the owner of the property in suit and that the Power of Attorney is not from a fictitious Jatindra Mohon Roy. It may be mentioned it was the case of the defendants that the plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy is not the Jatindra Mohon Roy who owned the property at 62 BCC Road and from whom Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui purchased the property. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff Respondent upon referring to the passport of Jatindra Mohon Roy (Ext.14) and the entries therein including the Visa and the endorsement showing Jatindra Mohon Roy's leaving Bangladesh has submitted that from the defendants' side there was no challenge as to the genuineness of the passport and the entries therein. It may be mentioned Jatindra Mahan Roy visited Bangladesh on the basis of a passport issued by the Government of India on July 26, 1978 and upon referring to the Ext.14 and the entries therein the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-Respondent has submitted that genuineness of the plaintiff Jatindra Mahon Roy was sufficiently established by the entries in Ext.14. Suffice it to say the passport and the entries therein are no doubt relate to the holder of said pass-port and even if for argument's sake it is accepted that said Jatindra Mohon Roy as plaintiff filed the suit but the fact is that it was not established by reliable evidence that plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy in the face of challenge from the side of the defence that the suit has been filed by the fictitious person is the real Jatindra Mohon Roy, who was the owner of the property at 62 BCC Road. The learned Counsel of the plaintiff- Respondent as. against the contention of defendants as to non-establishing of identity of plaintiff submitted that in the background of the case of the defense that suit has been filed by fictitious Jatindra Mohon Roy and not by the real Jatindra Mohon Roy, who sold his property to Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui, it was the duty of the defendants to take steps for production of plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy who visited Bangladesh on the basis of Ext.14 before the Court and in this connection the learned Counsel has referred to the proviso to Rule 1 of Order 3 and order 5 Rule 3 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The submission so made appears to be not well founded in law since provision in the proviso to Order 3 Rule 1 relates to compliance of order of the Court by any party for ' appearance in person and the other provision of Order 5 Rule 3(2) CPC relates to compliance of the order of the Court directing the plaintiff to appear in person before the Court on specified date. As per provision of law referred to above it is the Court that may require a party itself to appear before the Court. In the background of the challenge made as to the identity of the plaintiff it was the duty of the plaintiff to establish the fact that plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy was the real Jatindra Mohon Roy who owned the property at 62 BCC Road. Person who visited Bangladesh on the basis of Ext.14 was present in Bangladesh when the suit was ready for hearing. The plaintiff instead of taking steps for taking down his evidence in Court who visited the Court premises filed petition seeking permission for taking down his evidence on commission. The application so filed was contested by the defendants stating specifically that Jatindra Mohon Roy who figured as plaintiff was a fictitious person. In the afore state of the matter the plaintiff was required to establish the plaintiff was Jatindra Mohon Roy who owned the property in suit, but did not establish the same. 

 20. The learned Counsel of the plaintiff-Respondent in support of the contention that the identity of the plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy was established by the evidence on record has referred to the evidence of P. Ws. and D.W.3. P.W.I has stated that plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy who died on January 17, 1987 was his father in law and he gave him Power of Attorney to file and prosecute the suit and after plaintiffs death his heirs (5 sons) have been substituted and they have given him Power of Attorney (Ext.2) that Jatindra Mohon Roy mutated his name in respect of the property bearing holding No.62 BCC Road, that Jatindra Mohon Indian passport has been filed in Court and in the passport (Ext.14) there are signatures and the photo of Jatindra Mohon Roy. The evidence of P.Ws.2 and 3 has been noted hereinbefore. The learned Counsel has also referred to the statement of D.W.3 in cross-examination wherein he has identified the photo in the passport as of Jatindra and stated that Jatindra had no other name. This witness has also stated that it was not known to him whether name of Jatindra was Jatindra Mohon Roy and Jatindra was known to him and he was well educated man and he used to serve in the Bangladesh Bank, branch at, Sadar Ghat and it is not true that in the property in suit Jatindra Mohon Roy used to stay and in the said property none by name Sachindra used to live. The evidence so retie upon from plaintiff-Respondent's side in our view in no way has established the fact that plaints Jatindra Mohan Roy was the owner of the property at 62 BCC Road or in other words has dislodged the challenge of the defendants that plaintiff is a fictitious person and that he was not the owner of the property at 62 BCC Road, nor the plaintiff is the Jatindra Mohon Roy who sold the property at 62 BCC Road to All Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui. 

 22. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff-Respondent in summing up his submissions submitted that contention of the defendants as to non-establishing the identity of the plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy merits no consideration as defendants did not take any step to prove their case that plaintiff Jatindra Mohan Roy was a fictitious Jatindra Mohon Roy and not the real Jatindra Mohon Roy who sold the property at 62 BCC Road to Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui, that defendants have admitted ownership of the property at 62 BCC Road by Jatindra Mohon Roy, that the defendants have not taken step to prove their case that suit was filed by fictitious Jatindra Mohon Roy and that Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui purchased the property from Jatindra Mohon Roy who was the owner of the property at 62 BCC Road, that defendants did not take any step for producing plaintiff-Jatindra Mohon Roy in Court and did not press the petition filed with the prayer for making direction to the plaintiff to examine plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy's son and that no step was taken by the defendants to establish that Power of Attorney was executed by fictitious Jatindra Mohon Roy. Suffice it to say that it was the duty of the plaintiff to establish that plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy was the genuine Jatindra Mohon Roy who owned the property at 62 BCC Road and only thereafter it was the duty of the defendants to establish their case that the plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy was a fictitious person and the suit was not filed by real Jatindra Mohon Roy who owned the property at 62 BCC Road and sold the said property to Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui from whom the defendants purchased the property in suit. The other contentions are of no merit because of the established rule that at first plaintiff is to prove his case and then onus shifts upon the defendants to establish his contention or to disprove plaintiffs case. 

 35. The plaintiff, whose identity was seriously challenged, filed the suit seeking declaration of title in respect of the property in suit and for khas possession of the part of the suit property described in schedule 'B' attached to the plaint. The suit was filed on September 3, 1976. On July 10, 1988 the plaintiff filed an application seeking amendment of the plaint by way of insertion of some facts and the relief (b)(I) i.e. seeking declaration that the kabalas (Exts.9 and 9 `ka') dated October 27, 1969 in the name of Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui were forged, fraudulent and" not binding upon the plaintiff. Although aforesaid declaration was sought but the recipients of the said kabalas i.e. Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui were not impleaded in the suit. In that state of the matter it was the consistent contention of the appellants that the suit was bad for defect of parties for non-impleading the said 2 (two) persons. It may be mentioned that appellants while filed the written statement in February 1977 averred that the suit was bad for defect of party for non-impleading the Government of Bangladesh as well as Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui, the vendors of the contesting defendants. The plaintiff added the Government of Bangladesh in the category of defendants. It appears from the record of the suit that interrogatory was served on the defendants to furnish address of the persons who were not made party in the suit and defendants having not replied thereto the plaintiff filed an application with the prayer for debarring them from raising the plea of defect of party and the Court allowed the said prayer. The plaintiff filed an application seeking amendment of the plaint on July 10, 1988. The Court by the order dated November 19, 1988 allowed the prayer for amendment of the plaint and thereupon, amongst others, additional relief (b)(I) was inserted in the plaint seeking declaration that the deeds of 27th October, 1969 in the name of Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui were forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff. On the incorporation of relief (b) (I) the suit under went transformation making it obligatory for plaintiff, to implead the recipients of Exts.9 and 9 (ka) since those vendees became necessary parties and in their absence no legally sustainable decree be passed against them. On the incorporation of relief (b) (I) as the suit assumed the character different from pre-amendment the order debarring defendants from raising plea of defect of party passed prior to the amendment of plaint incorporating relief (b) (I) lost its force since with the amendment of plaint the vendees of Exts.9 and 9 (ka) who prior to amendment were neither necessary nor proper party, became necessary party and their particulars were very much available in Exts:9 and 9 (ka). 

 36. At all level the contesting defendants contended that the suit so far the same relates to (b) (I) i.e. seeking declaration that the deeds dated October 27, 1969 are forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff was bad for defect of party for non-Impleading the recipients of the said deeds. The admitted possession is that the recipients of the deeds of October 27, 1969 were not made party in the suit although relief was sought in respect of the said deeds. 

 37. The trial Court has not disposed of the contention of the defendants as regard defect of party for non-impleading the recipients of the deeds dated October 27, 1969 because of seeking declaration that the said deeds were forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 38. The High Court Division has disposed of the appellants' contention as to defect of parties for non-impleading the recipients of the kabalas dated October 27, 1969 upon observing that the defendant-appellants. were debarred from raising the question of non joinder of parties by the order dated 15.7.1986. It may be mentioned High Court Division was quite unmindful of the fact that relief (b)(I) i.e. declaration sought for that the deeds of October 27, 1969 were forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff Was inserted in the plaint in pursuant to the order dated November 19, 1988 allowing the petition dated July 10, 1988 seeking amendment of the plaint. 

 39. The plaintiff filed the suit on September 3, 1976 keeping in view the deeds dated October 27, 1969 and that later on got inserted the relief (b)(I) since in the absence of declaration as in relief (b)(1), the reliefs i.e. declaration of title and recovery of possession if allowed would not be a complete one. The undisputed position in law is that plaintiff cannot have a relief against a person who is not a party in the suit. In the instant case deeds of October 27, 1969 in respect of whereof relief has been sought by way of declaration that the said deeds were forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff were in the name of Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui or in other words the said two persons were the recipients of the deeds of October 27, 1969. Although relief sought in respect of the deeds of October 27, 1969 but the recipients of the same were not made party in the suit. The High Court Division was not correct in rejecting the contention of the defendants, that the suit so far the same relates to deeds of October 27, 1969 was bad for defect of party for non impleading the recipients of the said deeds as because the Court by the order dated July 15, 1986 debarred the defendants from taking the plea of defect of party in a different context and at a time when relief seeking declaration that the deeds of October 27, 1969 were forged and fraudulent were not the subject matter of the suit. 

 40. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff-Respondent has submitted that the defendants in their written statement filed in 1977 mentioned the names of the persons who were not made parties in the suit and thereupon plaintiff impleaded one of those and served interrogatory as regard the others but the defendants did not reply to the interrogatory and thereupon the Court made order debarring defendants from raising the plea that the suit is bad for defect of party. The learned Counsel also submitted that recipients of the deeds of October 27, 1969 (Exts.9 and 9 (ka)) were not necessary and proper party in the suit since they have transferred their interest to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and as such challenge to the validity of the deeds on the basis whereof defendant Nos. and 2 raised claim in the land in suit was in effect challenge to the document recipients whereof were Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui. The learned Counsel continued that determination of the validity or legality of documents on which defendants based their claim in the land in suit as well as the documents on the basis of which defendants' documents were made is germane in the background of the reliefs sought by way of declaration of title and recovery of possession. It was further submitted by the learned Counsel that because of the provision of Order 1, Rule 10 (2) read with order 22 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for non-impleading of Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui the suit cannot be said bad for defect of party. It has lastly been submitted by the learned Counsel that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 being the claimant of the land in suit were required to answer the issue raised in the suit since the recipients of the deeds dated October 27, 1969 divested their interest by selling the property of the said deeds to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and as such recipients of the deeds of October 27, 1969 were neither necessary nor proper party in the suit. 

 41. Provision of Order 22, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for continuation of a suit in the background of the situation given therein i.e. assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pendency of the suit. In the instant case none of the aforesaid situations are present and as such the said provision is of no assistance to the plaintiff-Respondent in rebutting the contention of the appellants that the suit so far the same relates to validity of the deeds dated October 27, 1969 for non-impleading the recipients of the said deeds is bad in law. The other contention that because of the provision of Order 1, Rule 10(2) the suit cannot be said bad for defect of party for non-impleading the recipients of the deeds dated October 27, 1969 is also not legally well founded since it was incumbent upon the plaintiff to implead the persons against whom, as in the instant case against the recipients of the deeds dated October 27, 1969, relief is sought. The contention that the recipients of the deeds dated October 27, 1969 were not necessary and proper party in the suit is also not legally sustainable since relief has been sought in respect of the documents recipients whereof were Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui and the suit was filed keeping in view the deeds of October 27, 1969 and as it appears plaintiff in November 1988 got the relief (b)(I), i.e. declaration that the deed of October 27, 1969 was forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff inserted in the pleading by amendment since the other relief s sought would not be complete in the absence of declaration in respect of the deeds of October 27, 1969. The other contention that challenge to the document of defendant Nos.1 and 2 was in effect challenge to the deeds dated October 27, 1969 and that reliefs by way of declaration of title and recovery of possession were germane in the determination of the documents on the basis whereof defendants raised claim in the land in suit is also not correct in that fact in the background whereof deeds of October 27, 1969 were made were known to the recipients of those and they were the competent persons to explain the situation in the background whereof they obtained the document from Jatindra Mohon Roy @ Sachindra Mohon Roy. Moreover plaintiff has sought relief against the deeds of October 27, 1969 recipients whereof Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui and as such they were very much required to be made parties in the suit since relief was sought against the documents whereby they acquired title in the land in suit. 

 42. The plaintiff after lapse of more than 12 years since the date of institution of the suit by way of amendment sought the relief (b)(I)i.e. declaration that the deeds of October 27, 1969 in the name of Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui were forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff and thus relief having in fact sought against the recipients of the deeds of October 27, 1969 (Ext.9 and 9 (ka) the said recipients became necessary party in the suit and a such plaintiff was required to implead them in the suit and that having not impleaded them the suit so far the same related to it the validity of the deeds of October 27, 1969 was bad for defect of party since they were necessary parties in presence of whom the relief sought in respect of the deeds of October 27, 1969 were required to be adjudicated. In this connection reference may be made to the decision in the case of Mt. Jahan Ara Begum Vs. Al. Md. Shamsul Hoque reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129 wherein it has been held "The position in law undoubtedly is that in the absence of a necessary party a decree cannot be made in favour of the plaintiff. Of course, the question as to what parties are necessary is often not easy to determine. One test which has been recognized as of great importance is that when in the absence of a party the court cannot give an effective remedy, that party is a necessary party. Besides, in order that a party may be considered a necessary party two conditions must be satisfied, first, that there must be a right to some relief against him in respect of the matter involved in the suit and, second, that his presence should be necessary in order to enable the court effectively and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit". The learned Counsel for the appellants in support of the contention that because of non-impleading the necessary party against whom the relief was sought by way of seeking declaration that the deeds of October 27, 1969 were forged, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff and thus the recipients of the said deeds became necessary party and they having not been impleaded the suit so far the same relates to the relief (b) (I) was bad for defect of party has referred to the case of Mohar Ali and others Vs. Zafar Ali and others reported in 27 MR, 451 wherein it has been observed "On the question of non-joinder of parties reference may be made to the provisions of Order 1 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in which it has been laid down that no objection on the ground of non-joinder of parties shall be given effect to unless it has been taken at the earliest possible opportunity and when such objection has not been so taken, it shall be deemed to have been waived. This question, however, is subject to another legal principle. It is no doubt true that the party to a suit shall not be allowed to agitate the question of non-joinder or misjoinder of parties at a subsequent stage if such a plea has not been taken at the earliest opportunity. But there is also another principle which has received judicial recognition, according to which no court shall pass an in fructuous decree. If it is found on a consideration of the evidence on record that a necessary party has not been impleaded in consequence whereof the decree which may be passed in the suit may be set at naught at the instance of the non-impleaded person, such a decree shall not be passed by a Court". 

 44. The trial Court held that by the deeds dated October 27, 1969 Jatindra Mahon Roy did not alienate his interest in the land in suit in favour of Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that in making the said finding the said Court placed reliance on the report of the Hand Writing Expert (Ext. 10). It may be mentioned Hand Writing Expert was not examined by the parties. In that view of the matter the trial Court was in serious error in making the judgment on the basis of the report of the Hand Writing Expert which was not admissible in evidence because of non-examination of the Expert who made the report. Moreover plaintiff’s identity was required to be established because of the definite case of the defendants that plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy is a fictitious person and that he was not the real Jatindra Mahon Roy alias Sachindra Mohon Roy who transferred the property in suit to All Ahmed Khandker and Wall Mohammad Siddiqui. We have already held that plaintiff miserably failed to establish the identity of Jatindra Mohon Roy who figured as plaintiff and allegedly was the owner of the property at 62 BCC road and it was not the Jatindra Mohon Roy alias Sachindra Mohan Roy who transferred the property in suit to the recipients of the deeds dated October 27, 1969. Of course plaintiff is not competent to raise the last plea since he having no interest in the land in suit not competent. It is also seen from the judgment of the trial Court that the said Court resorted to the mode as provides in section 73 of the Evidence Act and thereupon comparing signature in the pass port (Ext.14) and in the Power of Attorney (Ext. 1 'ka') with the signature appearing in the deeds .of October 27, 1969 held the document of October 27, 1969 forged. The mode so resorted to by the trial Court was erroneous since identity of the plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy whose signature claimed to be in Ext. 14, and Ext. 1 (ka), was not established in the background of the contention of the defendants that the said plaintiff is a fictitious Jatindra Mohon Roy and not the real Jatindra Mohon Roy who transferred the property in suit by the deeds dated October 27, 1969 to Ali Ahmed Khandker and Wali Mohammad Siddiqui. The High Court Division concurred with the finding and decision of the trial Court as regard the deeds dated October 27, 1969. Since the finding of the trial Court that by the deeds of October 27, 1969 plaintiff Jatindra Mohon Roy did not transfer the land in suit was arrived at on the basis of inadmissible evidence and upon resorting to a made whereof there was no basis, as such the said finding of the trial Court and the High Court Division was not legally sustainable.
